entry: Imaging technique using X-rays, gamma rays, or similar ionizing and non-ionizing radiation to view the internal form of an object. Applications include medical (diagnostic and therapeutic) and industrial radiography, as well as airport security, where "body scanners" generally use backscatter X-ray. In conventional radiography, an X-ray beam is projected through the object, and the rays that pass through are captured by film or a digital detector, producing a flat image called projectional radiography. In [[CT scan|computed tomography]], an X-ray source and detectors rotate around the subject, and the attenuated beams are computed into images on three planes that can be combined into a three-dimensional image. Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen discovered X-rays on November 8, 1895, and the first clinical use followed on January 11, 1896, when John Hall-Edwards radiographed a needle in an associate's hand in [[Birmingham]], England.

English rock band formed in Abingdon, Oxfordshire, in 1985. Its experimental approach is credited with advancing [[Alternative rock|alternative rock]]. *Kid A* (2000) marked a dramatic change in style, incorporating [[Electronic music|electronic music]], [[Jazz|jazz]] and [[Classical music|classical music]]; it divided listeners but was later named the best album of the decade by multiple outlets. As of 2011, the band had sold more than 30 million albums, and it has won six [[Grammy Awards]]. It was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2019.

Unicellular eukaryotes that produce intricate [[Mineral|mineral]] [[Skeleton|skeletons]], usually made of silica. Radiolaria are 0.1–0.2 mm in diameter and have a central capsule that divides the cell into an inner endoplasm and an outer ectoplasm. Needle-like pseudopods, supported by bundles of microtubules, help with buoyancy. They are found as zooplankton throughout the global ocean. They are primarily heterotrophic, but many have photosynthetic endosymbionts and are considered mixotrophs. Their skeletal remains make up a large part of the ocean floor as siliceous ooze. Because species change rapidly and their skeletons are intricate, radiolarians are an important diagnostic [[Fossil|fossil]] found from the [[Cambrian]] onward.

Medical specialty that uses [[Medical imaging|medical imaging]] to diagnose diseases and guide treatment in humans and other animals. It began with [[Radiography|radiography]] but now includes all imaging modalities, from ultrasonography and [[Magnetic resonance imaging|magnetic resonance imaging]] (MRI), which use non-ionizing acoustic or electromagnetic radiation, to computed tomography (CT), fluoroscopy and nuclear medicine, which use [[Ionizing radiation|ionizing radiation]]. Interventional radiology uses imaging guidance to perform usually minimally invasive procedures. A radiologist, a [[Medicine|medical]] doctor with specialized postgraduate training, interprets images and communicates findings to other physicians. Radiographers, called radiologic technologists in the United States and Canada, perform radiographic procedures and [[Radiation therapy|radiation therapy]] for the diagnosis and treatment of diseases such as cancer, and in some regions they also interpret images. Nurses care for patients before and after imaging and procedures.

Flowering plant in the mustard family, [[Brassicaceae]], cultivated for its large taproot. Domesticated in [[Asia]], radishes are now grown and eaten worldwide, and the entire plant is edible. They are often eaten raw in [[Salad|salads]], where their pungent, slightly spicy flavor comes from compounds including glucosinolate, myrosinase and isothiocyanate. Smaller varieties are ready within a month, while [[Daikon|daikon]] varieties take several weeks. Radishes are also grown as cover and forage crops, and some are grown for their seeds or for oil. Scientists tentatively place their origin in [[Southeast Asia]], the only region where truly wild forms have been found. Radishes enter the historical record in the third century BC.

Radioactive [[Alkaline earth metal|alkaline earth metal]], chemical element with atomic number 88 (Ra). Pure radium is silvery-white but readily reacts with nitrogen in air, forming a black surface layer. Its most stable isotope, radium-226, has a [[Half-life|half-life]] of 1,600 years. [[Marie Curie|Marie]] and [[Pierre Curie]] discovered radium in 1898 in ore mined at Jáchymov, and Marie Curie and André-Louis Debierne isolated the metal in 1910. Radium is [[Carcinogen|carcinogenic]] and accumulates in bones. Widely used in self-luminous paints after its discovery, it was replaced in nearly all applications by less dangerous radioisotopes. As of 2018, other than in nuclear medicine, it had no commercial applications; one of its few remaining non-medical uses is producing [[Actinium|actinium]] in [[Nuclear reactor|nuclear reactors]].

Colorless, odorless, radioactive [[Noble gas|noble gas]], chemical element with atomic number 86 (Rn). Its most stable isotope, radon-222, has a [[Half-life|half-life]] of 3.825 days. Because of this instability, radon is one of the rarest elements, but it is constantly regenerated in the decay chains of uranium and thorium. It was discovered in 1899 by [[Ernest Rutherford]] and Robert B. Owens at McGill University in [[Montreal]]. A common source is [[Uranium|uranium]]-containing minerals in the ground, and because radon is denser than air, it accumulates in basements. According to the United States Environmental Protection Agency, radon is the second most frequent cause of [[Lung cancer|lung cancer]] after [[Smoking|cigarette smoking]], causing 21,000 lung cancer deaths per year in the United States, about 2,900 of them among people who have never smoked.

Spanish former professional tennis player. He was ranked world No. 1 in men's singles for 209 weeks and won 22 [[Grand Slam (tennis)|major titles]], including a record 14 French Open titles. He also won two Olympic gold medals and is one of three men to complete the career Golden Slam in singles. His 81 consecutive wins on clay are the longest single-surface win streak in the Open Era. Nadal was a leading figure of the Big Three era alongside [[Roger Federer]] and [[Novak Djokovic]]. He retired after playing for Spain in the 2024 Davis Cup Finals.

Dominican military officer and dictator of the [[Dominican Republic|Dominican Republic]]. Trujillo ruled the country from August 1930 until his [[Assassination|assassination]] in May 1961, serving as president in 1930–38 and 1942–52 while holding the position of generalissimo, its de facto most powerful position. His 31-year rule, one of the longest for a non-royal leader, centered on a [[Cult of personality|personality cult]] around the ruling family. His security forces, including the SIM, were responsible for many murders, and in 1937 the Dominican Army killed Haitians on his orders in the Parsley massacre. Supporters credit him with stability and economic growth, while critics denounce the violence of his regime and the nepotism and corruption of his family.

Breed of large cat with a colorpoint coat and blue eyes. American breeder Ann Baker developed the Ragdoll in the 1960s. The breed is known for its docile, placid temperament and affectionate nature. Its name comes from its tendency to go limp and relaxed when picked up. Ragdolls are sometimes called dog-like cats because they follow people around, are receptive to handling and show relatively little aggression toward other pets. The breed is particularly popular in the [[United Kingdom|United Kingdom]] and the [[United States|United States]].

American rock band formed in Los Angeles in 1991. Its members were Zack de la Rocha, Tom Morello, Tim Commerford and Brad Wilk. The band blended heavy metal, rap, [[Punk rock|punk rock]], and [[Funk|funk]] with anti-capitalist and revolutionary lyrics. Its debut album, *Rage Against the Machine* (1992), was ranked No. 221 in 2020 on [[Rolling Stone|Rolling Stone]]'s list of the 500 greatest albums of all time. The band disbanded in 2000 and reunited in 2007. It influenced the [[Nu metal|nu metal]] genre and was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2023.

1980 American biographical sports drama film directed by [[Martin Scorsese|Martin Scorsese]]. Adapted from Jake LaMotta's 1970 memoir *Raging Bull: My Story*, it stars [[Robert De Niro|Robert De Niro]] as the former middleweight boxing champion, with [[Joe Pesci|Joe Pesci]] in a supporting role. The film received eight nominations at the 53rd Academy Awards, winning two, including Best Actor for De Niro. In 1990 it became the first film selected in its first year of eligibility for the National Film Registry, by the [[Library of Congress]]. In 2007 the American Film Institute ranked it the fourth-greatest American movie of all time.

Legendary Viking hero and king of Sweden and Denmark. He appears in Old Norse poetry from the [[Viking Age|Viking Age]], in Icelandic [[Saga|sagas]] and in near-contemporary chronicles. According to tradition, he conducted many raids against the [[British Isles|British Isles]] and the [[Carolingian Empire|Carolingian Empire]] in the 9th century. Some historians view him as a composite figure inspired by several 9th-century Viking chieftains rather than a single individual.

Musical style noted for its syncopated, or "ragged," rhythm. It originated in African American communities in the late 19th century and was popular from the 1890s to the 1910s, led by composers such as James Scott, Joseph Lamb and especially [[Scott Joplin|Scott Joplin]], the "King of Ragtime." Ragtime pieces, or "rags," usually contain several distinct themes and are typically composed for [[Piano|piano]]. The style influenced early [[Jazz|jazz]], Harlem stride piano and European composers such as [[Claude Debussy]] and [[Igor Stravinsky]]. Overshadowed by jazz in the 1920s, it was revived in the 1970s, when several of Joplin's songs were used in the film *The Sting*.

1981 American action-adventure film directed by [[Steven Spielberg|Steven Spielberg]]. The film stars [[Harrison Ford|Harrison Ford]] as Indiana Jones, an archaeologist who competes with Nazi German forces to recover the [[Ark of the Covenant|Ark of the Covenant]], said to make an army invincible. Set in 1936, it was written by Lawrence Kasdan from a story by [[George Lucas|George Lucas]] and Philip Kaufman. It was the highest-grossing film of 1981 and is the first entry in the Indiana Jones franchise. The [[Library of Congress]] selected it for the National Film Registry in 1999.

Cosmopolitan family of small to medium-sized birds (Rallidae), many associated with [[Wetland|wetlands]]. The family includes crakes, coots and gallinules, and it is found on every continent except [[Antarctica|Antarctica]] and in every terrestrial habitat except dry deserts, polar regions and alpine areas. Rails are weak fliers and common vagrants, which helped them colonize many isolated islands. Of roughly 150 historically known species, 31 extant or recently extinct species evolved flightlessness from flying ancestors. Rails have suffered disproportionately from human changes to the environment, and several hundred island species have become [[Extinction|extinct]]. The name, from French *râle*, refers to the birds' harsh cry.

Mode of land transport using wheeled vehicles that run on tracks, usually of two parallel steel rails. It is one of the two primary means of land transport, next to [[Road transport|road transport]], and it carries about 8% of passenger and [[Freight transport|freight]] traffic globally, thanks to its energy efficiency and potentially high speed. Rolling stock encounters lower [[Friction|friction]] than rubber-tired road vehicles, so trains can be coupled into longer loads. Modern rail transport began with the [[Steam locomotive|steam locomotive]] in the United Kingdom at the beginning of the 19th century, and railways were a key component of the [[Industrial Revolution|Industrial Revolution]]. The first passenger railway, the Stockton and Darlington Railway, opened in 1825. The first high-speed railway opened in Japan in 1964, and rail has revived in recent decades as governments invest in it to reduce CO₂ emissions.

Structure of a railway consisting of rails, fasteners, sleepers and ballast on a subgrade. Also called the permanent way, the track gives trains a dependable, low-friction surface on which steel wheels can roll. Early tracks used wooden or cast-iron rails and wooden or stone sleepers, and since the 1870s rails have almost universally been made of steel. The first railway in Britain, the Wollaton Wagonway, was built in 1603 with wooden rails. When [[Steam locomotive|steam locomotives]] appeared in 1804, the existing track proved too weak, and engineers later adopted flexible structures that allowed elastic movement. Most heavy-traffic lines now use continuously welded rails attached to sleepers with base plates, and timber sleepers are often treated with [[Creosote|creosote]].

Optical phenomenon in which [[Refraction|refraction]], internal reflection and dispersion of light in airborne water droplets form a multicolored arc in the sky. Rainbows can be caused by rain, mist, spray and airborne [[Dew|dew]], and those caused by sunlight always appear in the part of the sky directly opposite the sun. In a primary rainbow, [[Red|red]] is on the outer edge and [[Violet (color)|violet]] on the inner side. A double rainbow has a second arc about 10° outside the primary, with its colors in reverse order. Rainbows are usually seen in the western sky in the morning and the eastern sky in the early evening. From an aircraft, a rainbow can appear as a full circle. The longest-lasting rainbow recorded by [[Guinness World Records|Guinness World Records]] lasted 8 hours 58 minutes, in the Yangmingshan range of [[Taipei|Taipei]], [[Taiwan|Taiwan]], in November 2017.

Austrian poet regarded as a significant writer in the German language. Born in [[Prague|Prague]], then part of [[Austria-Hungary|Austria-Hungary]], he traveled widely through Europe before settling in [[Switzerland|Switzerland]], which inspired many of his poems. His work is acclaimed for its idiosyncratic and expressive style, and critics see undertones of [[Mysticism|mysticism]] and an exploration of subjective experience. In 1899 he met [[Leo Tolstoy|Leo Tolstoy]] in Moscow, and from 1905 to 1906 he was secretary to [[Auguste Rodin|Auguste Rodin]]. Among English-language readers his best-known works include *Duino Elegies*, *Sonnets to Orpheus* and the semi-autobiographical novel *The Notebooks of Malte Laurids Brigge*. He also wrote in French, and *Letters to a Young Poet*, a collection of ten letters, was published posthumously.

Forest characterized by a closed, continuous tree canopy, moisture-dependent vegetation, epiphytes and lianas, and the absence of wildfire. Rainforests are generally classified as [[Tropical rainforest|tropical]] or [[Temperate rainforest|temperate]], though other types have been described. Estimates vary from 40% to 75% of all biotic species being indigenous to rainforests. Tropical rainforests have been called the "jewels of the Earth" and the "world's largest pharmacy," because over one quarter of natural medicines have been discovered there. They are typically found within 10 degrees of the [[Equator|equator]] and receive average annual rainfall of no less than 168 cm (66 in). Although they have been called the "Earth's lungs," rainforests contribute little net oxygen to the atmosphere through [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]]. Rainforests are disappearing rapidly because of [[Deforestation|deforestation]], habitat loss and pollution of the atmosphere.

Capital and most populous city of the Indian state of [[Chhattisgarh|Chhattisgarh]]. Raipur is the administrative headquarters of Raipur district and a major commercial and industrial hub in Central India. It was part of [[Madhya Pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]] until Chhattisgarh was formed on November 1, 2000. The city is among India's biggest producers of steel and iron, with about 200 steel rolling mills, 195 sponge iron plants and at least six steel plants, and it has over 800 [[Rice|rice]] milling plants. Raipur has a tropical wet and dry climate. The district, like the rest of the Chhattisgarh plain, was once known as Dakshina Kosala and was considered to have been under the [[Maurya Empire|Maurya Empire]]. Raipur was ranked India's 6th cleanest city in the Swachh Survekshan for 2021.

Indian actor, filmmaker and producer in Hindi cinema. Born in [[Peshawar|Peshawar]], he was called "The Greatest Showman of Indian Cinema" and "The Charlie Chaplin of Indian Cinema." He was inspired by [[Charlie Chaplin|Charlie Chaplin]] and played Tramp-like characters in films such as *Awāra* (1951), *Shree 420* (1955) and *Mera Naam Joker* (1970). *Awāra* and *Boot Polish* (1954) competed for the Palme d'Or at the [[Cannes Film Festival|Cannes Film Festival]]. His films were commercial successes across Asia, the Middle East, Africa and the Soviet bloc. He received three National Film Awards and 11 Filmfare Awards. The [[Government of India|Government of India]] honored him with the Padma Bhushan in 1971, and he received the Dadasaheb Phalke Award, India's highest award in cinema.

[[Chola dynasty|Chola]] emperor who reigned from 985 to 1014. Also known as Rajaraja the Great, he conquered much of southern India and the Anuradhapura kingdom of [[Sri Lanka|Sri Lanka]], extending Chola influence across the Indian Ocean to islands including [[Lakshadweep|Lakshadweep]] and parts of the [[Maldives|Maldives]]. His campaigns also reached the Western Gangas and the Western Chalukyas, extending Chola authority as far as the Tungabhadra River. He commissioned the Rajarajeshwaram Temple in Thanjavur, a prominent example of medieval South Indian architecture and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In 1000 he began a land survey and assessment that reorganized the Tamil country into units called valanadus. He was succeeded by his son Rajendra Chola I.

State in northwestern India, the largest Indian state by area. It covers 342,239 square kilometers, or 10.4 percent of India's total area, and comprises most of the Thar Desert. It shares a border with [[Pakistan|Pakistan]] to the west and is bordered by five other states, including [[Gujarat|Gujarat]] and [[Madhya Pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]]. Its name, meaning Land of Kings, derives from [[Sanskrit|Sanskrit]] words for king and land. The state was formed on March 30, 1949, when the states of the Rajputana Agency of the erstwhile [[British Empire|British Empire]] merged into the Indian Union. Its capital and largest city is [[Jaipur|Jaipur]]. Major features include ruins of the [[Indus Valley Civilisation|Indus Valley Civilisation]] at Kalibangan, the Dilwara Temples, and Keoladeo National Park, a World Heritage Site known for its birdlife. Rajasthan has five national [[Tiger|tiger]] reserves.
